hub:alabama.rules:
Example: an Alabama personal injury claim, worked through

Say a careless driver or property owner injures you and you recover fully after a few months: $11,000 in medical bills and $4,000 in lost wages, with the other side claiming 10% of the fault is yours.

Medical bills and lost income$15,000
Pain and suffering (1.5× – 2× for a minor injury)$22,500 – $30,000
Claim before fault$37,500 – $45,000
Your 10% share of fault under Alabama’s ruleClaim barred
Estimated claim value$0

Under Alabama’s contributory negligence rule, that 10% share is enough to bar the claim in court, which is why the result is $0. If the insurer can’t prove any fault on your part, the same injury is worth about $37,500 – $45,000. That gap is why fault is the first thing adjusters fight over in Alabama.

The clock matters too: Alabama gives you two years from the injury to file suit, so for an injury on March 2, 2026 the last day would be March 2, 2028. Insurers know when that date is close.

Alabama injury claim rules

Fault. Alabama is one of only five places that still use contributory negligence. If you are found even slightly at fault, a court can bar your claim entirely. That makes proof of the other side’s fault, such as a police report, photos and witness statements, especially important. Narrow exceptions, such as the other driver’s wanton conduct or the last clear chance doctrine, can still allow recovery.

Filing deadlines. You have two years from the injury to file a personal injury lawsuit. Families have two years for a wrongful death claim, usually counted from the date of death. Claims against a government agency need written notice much sooner.

Car insurance. Alabama is an at-fault state, so the at-fault driver’s liability insurance pays your claim. Drivers must carry at least $25,000 per injured person, $50,000 per crash and $25,000 for property damage, written 25/50/25.

Damage caps. No cap on injury damages. Medical malpractice and punitive damages can have separate limits.

Dog bites. Owners are strictly liable for bites on their own property and for bites elsewhere if they knew the dog was dangerous.
hub:alabama.faqHtml:
Alabama injury claim questions

Can I still get a settlement in Alabama if I was partly at fault?

Usually not. Alabama uses contributory negligence, which can bar your claim if you were even slightly at fault. Narrow exceptions exist, so talk to a lawyer before giving up.

How long do I have to file a personal injury lawsuit in Alabama?

You have two years from the injury in most cases.

Who pays a personal injury settlement?

Usually the at-fault party’s insurer: auto, homeowner’s or business liability coverage. The policy limit often sets the practical ceiling.

What is the average injury settlement in Alabama?

No official source publishes a Alabama average, and averages hide a huge range. Value depends on your medical bills and lost income, how serious and lasting the injury is, your share of fault under Alabama’s contributory negligence rule and how much insurance is available. Does Alabama cap pain and suffering damages?

Example: an Alaska personal injury claim, worked through

Say someone else’s carelessness injures you and treatment runs for several months: $15,000 in medical bills and $5,000 in lost income, with the other side arguing you were 20% at fault.

Medical bills and lost income$20,000

Claim before fault$60,000 – $80,000
Your 20% share of fault under Alaska’s rule−$12,000 – −$16,000
Estimated claim value$48,000 – $64,000

Alaska uses pure comparative fault, so your 20% share cuts the award by 20% but never to zero. Even at 80% fault you would keep 20% of the value.

Alaska caps non-economic damages (from $400,000), but a limit that size only matters in far larger claims than this one.

If the claim settled at the midpoint of $56,000 with a lawyer on a 33⅓% contingency fee and about $1,100 in case costs, you would take home roughly $36,200, before repaying any medical liens.

The clock matters too: Alaska gives you two years from the injury to file suit, so for an injury on March 2, 2026 the last day would be March 2, 2028. Insurers know when that date is close.

Alaska injury claim rules

Fault. Alaska uses pure comparative fault. If a jury finds you 20% at fault, your award drops by 20%, and you can still recover something even if you were mostly to blame. Insurers still argue your share up, because every point of fault comes off the payout.

Filing deadlines. You have two years from the injury to file a personal injury lawsuit. Families have two years for a wrongful death claim, usually counted from the date of death. Claims against a government agency need written notice much sooner.

Car insurance. Alaska is an at-fault state, so the at-fault driver’s liability insurance pays your claim. Drivers must carry at least $50,000 per injured person, $100,000 per crash and $25,000 for property damage, written 50/100/25.

Damage caps. $400,000 or $8,000 times the injured person’s remaining life expectancy, whichever is greater. For severe permanent impairment or disfigurement, $1 million or $25,000 times life expectancy.

Dog bites. No dog bite statute. The owner is liable if they knew or should have known the dog was dangerous, or if they were negligent.

Insurance. Who pays depends on how you were hurt: auto insurance for a crash, a homeowner’s or business liability policy for an injury on someone’s property, or the at-fault party’s own assets when there is no insurance. The limit of that policy often sets the practical ceiling on a settlement.

Damage caps. No cap on injury damages. Medical malpractice and punitive damages can have separate limits.

Can I still claim if I was partly at fault in Michigan?
Yes. Your award is reduced by your percentage of fault. Above 50% you lose pain and suffering damages but can still recover reduced economic damages.
How long do I have to file a truck accident claim in Michigan?
You have three years from the crash to file a lawsuit. Report the claim to the insurers within days.
Do I need to meet a threshold to sue in Michigan?

Yes. Michigan is a no-fault state, so your PIP pays first. To claim pain and suffering from the at-fault driver you need death, serious impairment of a body function or permanent serious disfigurement.
What is the average truck accident settlement in Michigan?

No official source publishes a Michigan average, and averages hide a huge range. Value depends on your medical bills and lost income, how serious and lasting the injury is, your share of fault under Michigan’s 51% bar rule and how much insurance is available. Truck claims tend to be larger than car claims because injuries are more severe and trucking companies carry much higher insurance limits. The calculator above shows the math for your own numbers.
Does Michigan cap pain and suffering damages?
Not in most injury cases. No cap on injury damages. Medical malpractice and punitive damages can have separate limits.

Example: a Minnesota truck accident claim, worked through

Say a semi jackknifes on a wet highway and you can’t avoid it. A herniated disc needs an injection series and possible surgery: $36,000 in medical bills and $11,000 in lost wages so far, with the insurer blaming your following distance for 5% of the fault.

Medical bills and lost income$47,000
Paid first by your own PIP (no-fault)−$40,000
Pain and suffering (3× – 4× for a severe injury)$141,000 – $188,000
Claim before fault$148,000 – $195,000
Your 5% share of fault under Minnesota’s rule−$7,400 – −$9,750
Estimated claim value$140,600 – $185,250

Because 5% is under Minnesota’s 51% bar, the claim survives with a 5% cut. At 51% fault the same injury would be worth $0 in court.

Minnesota is a no-fault state, so your own PIP pays the first $40,000 of medical bills and lost income here, whoever caused the crash. You can claim pain and suffering from the at-fault driver only if the injury meets the threshold: $4,000 in medical bills (not counting diagnostic X-rays and rehabilitation), or 60 days of disability, a permanent injury or disfigurement, or death. If it doesn’t, PIP is usually your whole recovery.

Policy limits rarely cap a claim this size against a trucking company. Federal rules require interstate carriers hauling general freight to carry at least $750,000 of liability coverage (49 CFR § 387.9), and many carry far more.

If the claim settled at the midpoint of $162,925 with a lawyer on a 33⅓% contingency fee and about $3,300 in case costs, you would take home roughly $105,300, before repaying any medical liens.

The clock matters too: Minnesota gives you six years from the crash to file suit, so for an injury on March 2, 2026 the last day would be March 2, 2032. Insurers know when that date is close.

Minnesota rules behind this estimate

Fault. Minnesota uses modified comparative fault with a 51% bar. If you are found 20% at fault, your award drops by 20%. At 51% or more, you recover nothing. Insurers know this, so expect them to argue your share up.

Deadline. You have six years from the crash to file a lawsuit in Minnesota. Six years for negligence. Two years for intentional injuries such as assault. A claim against a city, county or state agency usually needs written notice much sooner, sometimes within months. Missing the deadline almost always ends the claim, and with it your leverage to settle.

Insurance. Minnesota is a no-fault state. Your own personal injury protection (PIP) pays your medical bills and part of your lost income first, up to $40,000: $20,000 for medical bills and $20,000 for income and other losses, whoever caused the crash. To claim pain and suffering from the at-fault driver, you need $4,000 in medical bills (not counting diagnostic X-rays and rehabilitation), or 60 days of disability, a permanent injury or disfigurement, or death. Liability minimums are 30/60/10.

Damage caps. No cap on injury damages. Medical malpractice and punitive damages can have separate limits.

Example: an Alabama slip and fall claim, worked through

Say you slip on an unmarked wet floor in a store and tear a knee ligament. Treatment costs $9,800, you miss $2,200 of work, and the store argues you were looking at your phone, putting 20% of the fault on you.

Medical bills and lost income$12,000
Pain and suffering (2× – 3× for a moderate injury)$24,000 – $36,000
Claim before fault$36,000 – $48,000
Your 20% share of fault under Alabama’s ruleClaim barred
Estimated claim value$0

Under Alabama’s contributory negligence rule, that 20% share is enough to bar the claim in court, which is why the result is $0. If the insurer can’t prove any fault on your part, the same injury is worth about $36,000 – $48,000. That gap is why fault is the first thing adjusters fight over in Alabama.

You also have to show the store knew or should have known about the spill and didn’t clean it up or warn you. The incident report, store video and how long the floor was wet often decide that.

The clock matters too: Alabama gives you two years from the fall to file suit, so for an injury on March 2, 2026 the last day would be March 2, 2028. Insurers know when that date is close.

Narrow exceptions, such as the other driver’s wanton conduct or the last clear chance doctrine, can still allow recovery.

Insurance. Slip and fall claims are paid by the property owner’s liability insurance: a homeowner’s policy for a house, or a commercial general liability policy for a store, restaurant or apartment complex. Business policies often carry $1 million or more.

Proof. You must show the owner knew or should have known about the hazard and did not fix it or warn you. Photos of the hazard, the incident report, store video and witness names carry the most weight.

Damage caps. No cap on injury damages. Medical malpractice and punitive damages can have separate limits.

What if I was partly at fault for the bite?
Yes, as long as you were less than 50% at fault. Your award is reduced by your percentage, and at 50% or more you recover nothing. Provoking or teasing the dog is the usual argument.
How long do I have to file a dog bite claim in Idaho?
You have two years from the bite to file a lawsuit. Report the bite to animal control and keep photos of the wound as it heals.
Who pays for a dog bite?
Usually the owner’s homeowner’s or renter’s insurance. Report the bite to animal control and get the owner’s insurance details at the scene if you can.
What is the average dog bite settlement in Idaho?

No official source publishes a Idaho average, and averages hide a huge range. Value depends on your medical bills and lost income, how serious and lasting the injury is, your share of fault under Idaho’s 50% bar rule and how much insurance is available. Nationally, insurers paid an average of $65,450 per dog-related injury claim in 2025, according to Triple-I and State Farm. The calculator above shows the math for your own numbers.
Does Idaho cap pain and suffering damages?
Yes. A cap on non-economic damages that started at $250,000 and is adjusted every July 1 for wage growth. It does not apply to willful or reckless conduct.

Alabama filing deadline examples

Here is how Alabama’s general rules play out on real dates. Count from the date of the injury, or the date of death for a wrongful death claim, unless an exception applies.

SituationLast day to file suit
Injured on March 2, 2026 (general personal injury)March 2, 2028
Family member died on June 15, 2026 (wrongful death)June 15, 2028

If the last day falls on a weekend or court holiday, the deadline usually moves to the next business day, but don’t plan around that. Filing early also protects you from the most common traps: a claim against a city, county or state agency, which usually needs a written notice of claim within months, and medical malpractice, which often runs on its own shorter clock.

Some rules can pause or extend the clock in Alabama, such as the injured person being a minor, the discovery rule for injuries found later, or the defendant leaving the state. They are narrow and fact-specific, so treat the date above as your real deadline unless a lawyer tells you otherwise.

Alabama filing deadlines

Personal injury. The general deadline is two years from the date of the injury.

Wrongful death. Families usually have two years, counted from the date of death.

Minors. Most states pause the deadline for an injured child until the child turns 18, though medical malpractice and government claims often follow shorter rules. Check how this applies before relying on it.

Government claims. A claim against a city, county, school district or state agency usually requires a written notice of claim within months, long before the lawsuit deadline.
